name: Chloe Okafor

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, and thanks for making the time. I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal week at university so far.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: A normal week is wild, in a good way. Lectures on cell biology and biochemistry, a lab on Tuesday where we grew bacteria that smelled awful, and a study group I started with six people from my corridor. I use an AI tutor all the time to quiz me before exams, and I've set up a little system that turns my lecture notes into flashcards. I'm in a hall of residence, I volunteer at a science outreach club for school kids on Saturdays, and I call my mum, who's a pharmacist, most evenings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, fine, the tools are useful but they won't change the world. I'd tell my study group to keep using them anyway, because even a small time-saver adds up over a degree. Online I'd probably post a funny screenshot of the tutor getting a biochemistry question wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'd be a little disappointed. I'd quite like the future to be exciting, and a plateau means my path is just a normal one. But it's also comforting: I'd go into research the way people always have, and my parents would know what to expect.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on exactly as I am. Study group, lab, outreach club, and the AI tutor for exam practice. I'd apply for a summer research placement in a neuroscience lab, which is where I'd love to end up, and I'd start reading papers early.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, a bit flat. I feel fine about my money and my place because my parents pay for everything and I have strong grades. The only wobble is whether I'm good enough for research, and no scenario changes that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would a plateau feel like a letdown, given how much you use these tools?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Funding for science, honestly. Research jobs depend on grants, and grants dry up for no reason. A plateau doesn't fix that, and I'd like the government to treat research as something worth paying for in the good years and the bad.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you still want to be different, even if little changes?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit, yes. I'm used to being the person who says the future is arriving, and a plateau makes me look silly for a while. But I'd rather be wrong and employed than right and unemployed, so I'd happily look silly for a while if the hype fades.

say: I'd say the tools are **useful**, but won't change the world.
I'd post a funny screenshot of my AI tutor getting **biochemistry** wrong.
think: Privately I'd be **a little disappointed**, because I like the idea of a thrilling future.
I'm comforted that my path into **research** would stay familiar.
do: Keep up the study group, lab and **outreach club**, plus AI exam practice.
Apply for a summer placement in a **neuroscience lab** and read papers early.
feel: **Calm**, a bit flat, with one wobble about being good enough.
S0.quote: I'd rather be wrong and employed than right and unemployed, so I'd happily look silly for a while if the hype fades.
fieldNote: She admits **mild disappointment** at a plateau, showing her appetite for change.
Her only wobble is **research funding**, a worry that exists without AI.
Calm comes from **family money** and top grades, which she names.

steps.text: Keep running the study group and the Saturday outreach club
Use the AI tutor for exam practice and check its answers against my textbook
Apply for a summer neuroscience lab placement

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the moment to learn the tools properly and not be scared of them. I'd tell friends who avoid AI that they're making it harder for themselves, but I'd also say that companies need rules so people aren't pushed out unfairly. I'd put both points in the same post, which makes people argue.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I think I'm well placed, but not safe. A lot of lab work today is data analysis and writing, which are exactly the tasks the systems take first. I'd still be needed for judgement and for designing experiments, but there'd be fewer entry roles to start from.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn programming and data analysis, probably Python, on top of my degree, and pick modules in bioinformatics. I'd offer to help my lecturers with something small, like a pilot where students use AI in a lab report, because showing I'm useful to a professor is how you get a placement. I'd also talk to my mum about how pharmacies are changing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited and a bit uneasy, like riding a fast bike downhill. I think I'd enjoy it, but I'd be looking at the road all the time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You already use AI every day. What would change for you in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: People who do routine lab work or repetitive data tasks, and they might not have my parents' safety net. A technician at my university told me she's worried about her contract. I'd want funding for retraining for people like her, not just warm words.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who in your life would be hit harder than you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be a person who can use the tools and also explain their limits, which is a real skill. If I'm good at that, I can work in a research team or a health firm. Being the person who knows how to check the system is a safer job than being the person it replaces.

say: I'd say it's the moment to **learn the tools** and also demand fair rules.
I'd tell friends who avoid AI that they're **making it harder** for themselves.
think: Privately I'm **well placed**, but not safe, because analysis and writing are taken first.
I expect **fewer entry roles** in labs even if judgement stays.
do: Learn **Python** and bioinformatics on top of my degree.
Offer a lecturer a small **AI lab-report pilot** to get noticed for a placement.
feel: **Excited and uneasy**, like a fast bike downhill.
S1.quote: Being the person who knows how to check the system is a safer job than being the person it replaces.
fieldNote: She sees her **edge as a checker** of AI, not a user of it.
She cares about the **lab technician** she knows, widening her view beyond herself.
Excitement and unease show up together, and she names both.

steps.text: Learn Python and take a bioinformatics module this year
Offer a lecturer a small pilot of AI-assisted lab reports
Back retraining funds for lab technicians by signing petitions and voting

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need to slow down and make a plan, because this is too fast for families to cope. I'd go to the student union and ask them to demand an emergency statement from the university. And I'd post one calm thing online, not a panic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be rattled. I'd be in second year when AI can do most thinking work, and my whole plan, a degree, a masters, a research job, has years in it. I'd wonder what research even is if a machine can read every paper and design experiments faster than I can.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd throw myself into learning everything: automation of lab work, how the systems are trained, who regulates them. I'd start a group on campus with other students to talk through options, because being alone with this is the worst part. I'd ask my parents about savings, and whether I should stay at university or work on something more immediate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd feel like I'm on a runway and the plane is already moving. I'd try to turn the fear into energy, but I'd lose sleep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Two years: what is the first day like for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, listen, whatever happens, you can learn how this works, and being curious is the best protection. I'd make sure she keeps her options open, and doesn't rush into a degree that assumes things won't change. I'd try to sound calmer than I feel.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you tell your younger sister?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Partly because I use it every day, so I know how good it already is. Being close to the tool makes the fear more concrete, because I look at what it does for my lecture notes and think, in two years that does everything.

say: I'd say we must **slow down and plan**, because this is too fast.
I'd ask the student union to demand an **emergency statement** from the university.
think: Privately I'd be **rattled**: my years-long plan would be shaken.
I'd wonder **what research is** if a machine reads every paper.
do: Start a campus group with other students to **talk through options**.
Ask my parents about **savings** and whether to stay at university.
feel: **Alarmed**, like a plane already moving on the runway.
S2.quote: Being close to the tool makes the fear more concrete, because I look at what it does for my lecture notes and think, in two years that does everything.
fieldNote: Daily use makes her fear **specific**, not vague.
She turns anxiety into **organising a group**, a hallmark of her adaptive style.
She tries to **sound calmer** than she feels when speaking to her sister.

steps.text: Start a campus group where students talk through options together
Learn how lab automation and model training actually work
Ask my parents whether to stay in my degree or switch to something sooner
Ask the student union to demand an emergency statement from the university

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we have time, and the smart move is to prepare now rather than argue about whether it's real. I'd bring it up in my lab group and ask what skills they'd want from a new person. I'd share my study-group notes, which might help some people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'd feel energised. Five years is enough to finish the degree, do a masters, and get some real research experience. I'd probably be in a good position, maybe leading a small team in a lab with automated equipment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd build a mix of skills: biology, data, and some policy knowledge so I can talk to regulators. I'd apply for every summer placement I can, start a masters plan, and keep a side project going, maybe a tool that helps students check AI answers. I'd also keep my savings sensible and not get carried away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious but in a useful way. I'd keep checking the news, and I'd probably over-plan, but I'd feel I had options. It's like having a map with a few missing roads.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With five years, what do you do differently from the two-year case?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the research job itself is gone, yes. But I think there'd be a role for people who ask good questions and decide what to study, even when the machine does the lab work. I'd keep going unless it became obvious that humans weren't needed at all.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there a point at which you'd drop research?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Policy. Understanding the rules around these systems gives you a seat at the table, and I think I'd enjoy it. I'd rather help decide how these systems are used than stand outside complaining about them.

say: I'd say we have time, so **prepare now** instead of arguing about whether it's real.
I'd share my **study-group notes** with anyone who wants them.
think: Privately I'd feel **energised**, because five years fits a degree, a masters and real experience.
I might end up **leading a small team** in an automated lab.
do: Build biology, data and **policy skills** so I can talk to regulators.
Apply for **every summer placement** and start a side project that helps students check AI answers.
feel: **Anxious but useful**, like holding a map with a few roads missing.
S3.quote: I'd rather help decide how these systems are used than stand outside complaining about them.
fieldNote: Her energy comes from **a plan**, which keeps anxiety productive.
She adds **policy** as a new interest, showing real adaptability.
She draws a line at **humans not needed**, her limit for research.

steps.text: Add a policy and regulation module to my biology and data skills
Build a small side project that helps students check AI answers
Apply for a summer research placement every year
Keep my savings sensible and save from my allowance

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift if we use it well. I'd tell people not to panic but not to coast, either. Every generation has been told the machines are coming, and I'd rather be the one holding the controller than the one watching from the doorway. I'd probably give a short talk at the outreach club about how kids should learn to be curious and check things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'm excited. By 2036 I'd be 29 with a PhD, maybe, and working at the same time the new tools are fully arriving, which feels like the best moment to be in science. I'd feel lucky, which I'd also feel guilty about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go for it fully: degree, masters, a PhD if the funding is there, and a lot of reading about how the systems work. I'd also hedge a little by learning enough about health policy to move there if research dries up. I'd keep my AI habit but add a rule to always check the source.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm and curious. It would feel like standing at the edge of something big but with a seatbelt on. I'd still get nervous about exams, but not about the future.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ten years is a long runway. Do you go for it fully, or hedge?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd hedge lightly. Learning policy or data is cheap compared with the benefit, and I'd probably enjoy it anyway. I'd just avoid becoming someone with a thousand half-finished courses.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who or what do you blame if it goes badly?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly companies that rush products out without checking, and governments that wait for a crisis before acting. I'd blame myself a little too. Staying silent isn't neutral, so I'd speak up now, and I'd blame myself a little if I stayed quiet when I could have helped.

say: I'd say ten years is a gift, so **don't panic**, don't coast.
I'd give an outreach-club talk on kids learning to **check things**.
think: Privately I'm **excited**, since 2036 would find me at the start of a science career.
I'd feel **lucky**, and a bit guilty about it.
do: Go for it fully: degree, **masters** and a PhD if funding is there.
Learn enough **health policy** to move sideways if research dries up.
feel: **Calm and curious**, like standing at the edge of something big with a seatbelt on.
S4.quote: Staying silent isn't neutral, so I'd speak up now, and I'd blame myself a little if I stayed quiet when I could have helped.
fieldNote: The long runway moves her to **calm**, with optimism tied to effort.
She includes **self-blame** for staying silent, which is unusual.
She **hedges lightly** with policy knowledge rather than leaving research.

steps.text: Study through a masters and a PhD if funding is there
Learn how the systems work and always check sources
Speak up in public debates and vote for sensible AI rules

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one, for sure, because I'd have barely started and everything I'm learning would be shifting under me. What would help is a place to go where people tell us honestly what's changing and what to learn, and some kind of income safety net. I'd also love universities to teach us how to work with these systems, not pretend they don't exist.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: I'd say don't assume that young people who use AI every day are lazy or cheating. I use it to learn faster, and I check it, and sometimes it teaches me something my lecturer skipped. If anything, I want my lecturers to use it in front of us so we can talk about when it's wrong.

headlineQuote: Every generation has been told the machines are coming, and I'd rather be the one holding the controller than the one watching from the doorway.
portrait: Chloe is 19, studying **biomedical science** with top results, a strong cushion and a plan to do research.
She is progressive and adaptive: she uses AI tools **every day** and starts new ones before her friends do.
She trusts **public support and regulation**, and thinks universities should teach people to work with AI.
She is excited and anxious in turn, and her mood rises and falls with **how much time** the warning gives.
Her mother, a pharmacist, and her study group are her base, and she acts by learning, joining and organising.
biggestWorry: The **2028 scenario** worries her most, because everything she is learning would shift before she can build a base.
whatWouldHelp: **Honest guidance** from universities on what is changing and what to learn.
Some form of **income safety net** while people retrain.
